name: Aull Block #1 & #2
development_era: 1906 to 1913 (Pre WWI Boom, Age of Optimism)
significance_summ:
This structure was constructed in two phases in 1908 and 1925 and is a typical, representative example of combined commercial and residential development of the period.  The easternmost, two storey brick structure, called the Shepard Block,  was completed in 1908 during Calgary's initial, pre-World War I boom and featured retail uses at grade with apartments and/or offices above. The property was purchased by Dr. E. Aull in 1911 and converted into possible the earliest medical consultancy centre in Calgary.

In 1925 Dr. Aull expanded the building and replaced the existing corner structure with current commercial building.  Aull Block #1 and #2 form a familiar corner landmark in the community.

name: Metals Limited Warehouse
development_era: 1919 to 1929 (Post WWI to Stock Market Crash)
significance_summ:
This site is significant because....

It is a high-quality and characteristic example of the plain Commercial style of architecture in the Beltline from the late 1920s.  Minimally adorned, its functional appearance and character define the building.  (Style value: Community Historic Resource).

Its contribution to Calgary's historic wholesale/warehouse district, recalls Calgary's historic status as the most important wholesale and distribution centre between Winnipeg and Vancouver. (Activity value: city-wide significance)

It helps to recall and define the semi-industrial character of the northern Beltline as the city's historic warehouse and wholesale centre (Symbolic value: Community Historic Resource).
significance_stmt_dscrn: This building was originally constructed in 1928 as a four-storey rectangular reinforced concrete and brick warehouse.  Designed in the Commercial warehouse style, it features a plain façade with brick pilasters, concrete lintels, and large windows.  Four additional storeys were added in 1998, largely in keeping with the original style.  The building is situated in Calgary's secondary warehouse district, on the corner of 11th Avenue and 2nd Street SW.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
This building has heritage value as a high-quality and characteristic example of the plain Commercial warehouse style of the late 1920s.  Built from locally sourced materials and almost completely fireproof, it was considered to be of superior quality at the time of its construction.  It features reinforced concrete floors, slab and beams, with steel frame window openings and solid brick walls.  Bays of large windows with concrete lintels are set between vertical brick piers, which define the overall look of the façade and serve to express the building's internal structure.  Whereas before the First World War most warehouses had some concession to ornament, by the late 1920s there was no effort to hide the building's purpose, reflected in its functional appearance and minimal ornamentation.  

Originally a plumbing supplies warehouse, this structure also has heritage value in symbolizing Calgary's rise as an important regional hub for wholesaling and warehousing prior to the First World War and to a lesser extent afterward.  In 1902 the CPR reduced its freight rates out of Calgary, establishing the city as the main distribution centre between Winnipeg and Vancouver.  The number of jobbers in Calgary rose from 80 in 1907 to about 150 by 1911, most of which were clustered along 10th and 11th Avenues.  The area experienced a more modest wave of development in the late 1920s, during a brief economic resurgence in Calgary.

This building was constructed for Metals Limited in 1928.
Incorporated in 1904 as the Gurney Standard Metals Co., Metals Limited was the first wholesaler of plumbing and heating supplies between Winnipeg and Vancouver.  The company also serviced the oil industry after the establishment of Turner Valley oil and gas field.  With W.R. Hull as its first president, Metals Limited had several prominent Calgary business leaders as officers and directors, including A.E. Cross, R.B. Bennett, Sir James Lougheed, and Senator Pat Burns.  In 1948 Metals Limited was acquired by Empire Brass Manufacturing Ltd., which, along with its associated firms, occupied the building until 1969.  

The Metals Limited warehouse also recalls and defines the semi-industrial character of the northern Beltline as the city's historic warehouse and wholesale centre.  With easy access to the CPR's mainline just over one block to the north, a string of warehouses developed along a corridor that came to be known as the warehouse district. Rail networks were physically integrated with the warehouses, with spurs running along the wide alley between 10th and 11th Avenues.  These spur lines serviced the warehouses in the area and permitted direct access to railway cars shunted from the main line.  The raised loading bay at the rear west side of the Metals Limited warehouse was built to accommodate access to freight train cars.  

From 1972 to 1993 the building was occupied by the landmark Calgary furniture store, Cristy's Arcade.  This business was successively owned by Abraham and Hyman Belzberg, both prominent members of Calgary's Jewish community.  After Cristy's closure the warehouse remained vacant for several years before its renovation in 1998 for use as a retail and office building.

integrity_stmt:
This originally four-storey structure was significantly altered in 1998 when four additional floors, designed by Gibbs Gage, were added.  At the same time, a substantial one-storey extension on the west side of the building was removed, as were brick and concrete parapets from each corner of the roof. The actual window openings were widened to extend the full width of the bays between vertical brick piers, new metal frames were installed, and the multi-pane windows were all replaced with plate glass.  A historic type roofline and storefront cornice were added during this time as well.  At the rear of the building, the elevator penthouse was removed and one loading door opening was in-filled at the east side.  

Some time after 1950, awnings were added to the first floor, and these were replaced with new awnings in 1998.  

Despite these significant modifications, the building retains good overall integrity.

name: Davis Residence
significance_summ:
- It is one of the oldest houses in the community and serves to recall that 12 Avenue in the Beltline was once a desirable (predominantly) residential street lined with substantial houses. (Symbolic value - Community significance)
- It exemplifies the Queen Ann revival style of architecture constructed in the Beltline neighbourhood. It is characterized by a hipped roof with cross gables, front and side bay windows and a full width front verandah  with classical-style columns. (Style value-Community significance)
significance_stmt_dscrn: The Davis Residence is a Queen Anne Revival-style dwelling that was built c. 1905. It is a two-storey wood-frame structure, placed on a sandstone foundation. Clad in lapped siding, it features a full-length front verandah and second-storey balcony, a hipped-roof with cross-gables, and bay windows.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
This property is symbolically significant as a rare remaining example of the attractive and substantial residential character that historically defined 12 Avenue in this part of the Beltline area, formerly known as Victoria Park. At the beginning of the twentieth century, many similar houses were built in the area for the professional, and middle classes.  Today, the Davis Residence survives as one and the few houses in this area, and is the only remaining house along 12 Avenue within a six-block vicinity. As the second-oldest known house to remain in the northern part of the Beltline it recalls the early development history of the area. 

Prior to the First World War, the length of 12 Avenue in the Beltline was almost entirely residential, except around the 1st Street intersection, and the block to the east, which were developed for commercial and retail use.  The 200 block of 12 Avenue West, where the Davis Residence is situated, included comfortable and attractive houses, such as this, and similar to those further east on 12 Avenue.  Beginning with the Davis Residence, the commercial and residential mixed-use 200 block of 12 Avenue West marked a transition zone where such residential properties immediately transitioned to more substantial and elaborate properties as the street proceeded west and approached Central Park.  Beyond 4th Street, Twelfth Avenue entered the neighbourhood once known as Connaught, and (along with 13 Avenue) was one of the most exclusive residential streets in the city prior to the development of the Mt. Royal district after 1906.   

The Davis Residence exemplifies the attractive and comfortable Queen Anne Revival-style houses built in Calgary at the beginning of the twentieth century. While some more-elaborate variants of the style survive in the city, the Davis Residence represents the version more commonly and widely constructed for the middle and professional classes. Once relatively common in the Beltline, Queen Anne Revival-style houses have become rare in the community.

Characteristic of the Queen Anne Revival style, the Davis Residence features a full-width front veranda that incorporates a second-storey porch, a hipped roof with lower cross gables, decorative-shingle-clad gables, bay windows, and leaded and stained glass window detailing. With a high level of integrity,  the house retains its original cladding and one-over-one windows. Additionally, the interior retains numerous features typical of the style such as a staircase with elaborately turned balusters, a highly ornamental fireplace surround, pocket doors, and some window and door casings. A secondary staircase at the rear of the house for servant use distinguishes the house as being somewhat more substantial and upper-end than most other houses being constructed in Calgary at the time.  

Construction of this dwelling is attributed to its first owner, Joseph William Smith, a carpenter and caretaker at Central Methodist Church. As a church caretaker, his needs for such a substantial dwelling indicate that the house was speculatively developed by Smith.  Emma Davis, and Edward Davis - a horse dealer and rancher - owned the residence from 1910-1945, but resided there intermittently (1911, 1914-1919, 1935-42). 

During the Davis¿ period of ownership, the house served several purposes. From 1912-1913, furnished rooms in the house were let by a Mrs. Clipsham, reflecting Calgary's acute housing shortage during the pre- First World War boom. Then, for a brief period after the war, the residence served as an annex to the adjacent YWCA building. During the Second World War, it was a nursing and rest home. Frank Patton, who was a long-time tenant, ran a garage and auto body shop at the rear of the residence for many years during the 1920s-40s.

name: Edmonds Block
development_era: 1906 to 1913 (Pre WWI Boom, Age of Optimism)
significance_summ:
This site is significant because:
- it contributes to the historic status of the 1 Street SW corridor as one of the city's early principal commercial and retail areas. It is an integral component of the 1 Street SW streetscape and recalls the area's historical character and function. (Symbolic value - Community significance)
- it is an attractive example of Edwardian Commercial style architecture, featuring a high-quality wraparound façade clad in buff-coloured brick, sandstone detailing and elegant finishes such as a Neoclassical-style fanlight (Style value - Community significance)
significance_stmt_dscrn: The Edmonds Block is a two-storey, flat-roof, Edwardian Commercial-style building of brick  and semi-milled construction. Built in 1913, it features a buff-brick  façade with sandstone ornamental detailing. The property is located immediately south of downtown in the Beltline area. It contributes to the concentration and streetscape of historic commercial buildings along and adjacent to 1 Street SW.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
The Edmonds Block, built in 1913, contributes to the historic status of the 1 Street SW corridor as one of the city's early principal commercial and retail areas. As an integral component of the 1 Street SW streetscape it recalls and symbolizes the area's historical character and function. 

Prior to First World War, 1 Street SW was developed to vie with the streets in the downtown core (north of the CPR tracks) as a primary retail and commercial zone. The street featured major department stores, banks, a variety of retail shops, offices and services. As part of the streetcar route, 1 Street SW was a heavily travelled thoroughfare leading into the downtown core making it a city-wide rather than a neighbourhood commercial zone.

Dr. Robert Franklin Edmonds, a dental surgeon, constructed the namesake building to house his offices as well to generate rental income from the additional ground floor offices and second-storey residential suites. From 1909-13 Calgary experienced an unprecedented population and economic boom leading to an acute shortage of commercial and residential space. During this boom period, Dr. Edmonds took a leave-of¿absence from the dental profession for several years to focus on the more lucrative real estate development business, serving as an executive with J.O.E. Ltd., a real estate and financial brokerage firm. In addition to Edmonds¿ own dental office, and his separate real estate office, the ground floor housed several other dental and doctors¿ offices, making the Edmonds Block somewhat of a `professional building¿. The second floor was divided into residential suites attracting working and middle-class occupants. 

The Edmonds Block is valued as an attractive example of Edwardian Commercial style architecture and features a high-quality wraparound façade clad in buff-coloured brick. The brickwork is laid with deeply recessed mortar joints and comprises soldiered window casing and decorative insets. Unlike most buildings from the period which are ornamented with lower-cost pressed-metal detailing, the Edmonds Block features sandstone detailing. Carved sandstone forms the roofline cornice and curved hood above the main entrance while smoothly finished sandstone comprises the storefront cornice, pier capitals and bases. An elegant Neoclassical-style fanlight tops the main entrance. Inside, the building was designed with an Arts and Crafts aesthetic with the focal point being a darkly stained wooden staircase with thick, squared, connected balusters. The walls of the staircase and the stair hall were finished with a complementary wood and plaster dado; hardwood floors lined the corridors.

integrity_stmt:
The most significant intervention is the infilling of the storefront which, although easily reversible, dramatically alters the building's appearance. Other exterior changes include the removal and replacement of the main façade's original window sashes, and the removal and replacement of some of the wooden sashes from the other facades. Additionally some of the window openings on the side and rear facades have been infilled, while the main entrance doors have been replaced with utilitarian steel doors.
Regarding the condition of the building's materials, some of the sandstone - especially that of the pier bases - has deteriorated significantly while deterioration has also begun to affect the entrance hood. Also, some of the main façade¿s brickwork has been painted (likely to cover graffiti) including that of the lower portion of the piers and the brick above the roofline cornice. 
The interior was not accessed, so its integrity is unknown. As of August 2007 the interior features described in the Statement of Significance were extant. It is unlikely that any of the ground floor's original layout remains. 
In early 2011 the building was condemned for habitation due to mold and pest infestation issues.

name: YWCA
development_era: 1906 to 1913 (Pre WWI Boom, Age of Optimism)
significance_summ:
This site is significant because...

As a shelter, leisure and recreation facility operated by the YWCA, and as an office space for social agencies and community organizations since 1971, the building has played a significant and continuous role in the provision of community services for Calgarians (Activity Value, City-Wide) 

It is associated with the Young Women's Christian Association, which built and occupied the building from 1911 to 1971 (Institution Value, City-Wide)

It is associated with a number of women involved in the building's establishment and operation, including Emily Kerby, Katherine Underwood, Elizabeth McDougall, Alice Jamieson, Jessie 'Chappie' Chapman and Joan Nelson (Person Value, City-Wide) 

It is elegant refined example of the Georgian Revival style of architecture in Calgary (Style Value, City-Wide)

The building symbolizes the brisk pace of growth during Calgary's 1909-1913 real estate boom, and the social dislocations which accompanied that growth (Symbolic Value, City-Wide)
significance_stmt_dscrn: The YWCA (Young Women's Christian Association) building is a three-story red brick and sandstone building constructed from 1910-1911 in the community of Beltline. A handsome example of the Georgian Revival style of architecture in Calgary, the building is distinguished by its symmetrical façade with dressed sandstone detailing, and a prominent three-storey veranda.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
The building is significant as a refined example of Georgian Revival style architecture in Calgary. Characteristic of the style, the building features a low-profile hip roof, symmetrical façade and modest classical detailing. The red-brick façade is enlivened with sandstone features including a prominent, rusticated foundation, quoins, pilasters, doorway surrounds and other decorative stone features. The classical pressed metal roofline cornice and low pediment further contribute to the building's character. The style extends to the interior with the classical but restrained detailing of the entrance hall and main staircase with its original balustrades. Dominating the entrance is an open, three-storey, wood veranda supported by classical columns, although not characteristic of Georgian Revival.   

The YWCA building has value related to the Young Women's Christian Association, its occupant from 1911 to 1971. The YWCA of Calgary, established in 1907, operated a hostel from a leased building until the Board of Directors raised funds to purchase six lots on 12th Avenue SW, and Alberta¿s first YWCA building opened in 1911. With a strong Christian mandate, the YWCA offered programs aimed at the mental, physical, spiritual and social development of girls and women.

Designed to provide safe accommodation for about 60 young women, the YWCA serves as a symbol of the pace of growth during Calgary's 1909-1913 boom, and the social dislocations that accompanied rapid urbanization. The YWCA was immediately filled to capacity as women flocked from rural areas to take up work in Calgary, and an annex in the Underwood Block (1311 1 ST SW) operated from 1911 to 1919. The YWCA also began an employment bureau for women in 1911 - a role it extended during the 1930s Depression - and in 1912, began a Travellers' Aid service to assist newcomers arriving by train to Calgary.

The YWCA building has value relating to its continuous role in providing community services. In its early years, the YWCA advocated for women's suffrage, health education, minimum wages and better working conditions. During the Second World War, the YWCA housed members of the Canadian Women's Army Corps, and ran a Blue Triangle service centre; the organization also helped resettle war brides following both World Wars. Over the decades various clubs for teenaged girls, young married women, and Aboriginal girls met in the building, as did the first Girl Guide troop west of Toronto. 

The YWCA also offered programs to the broader community, notably swimming lessons in the basement pool and language instruction for new Canadians. A new gym and swimming pool opened in an annex to the east in 1954. By the late 1960s the building remained overcrowded and in poor repair, and the YWCA opened a new facility in 1971 (5 AV SE). As a city-owned building, the 'Old Y Centre' continued to provide community services through low-cost office space for social service and cultural organizations. Faced with the building's demolition, some 23 tenants formed a society in 1979 to manage and preserve the building, which continues to serve a strong community role as the CommunityWise Resource Centre.  

The YWCA has value for its association with women who were involved in its establishment and operation. Emily Kerby was instrumental in founding a YWCA branch in Calgary and led the group's early fundraising efforts, and Katherine Underwood served as president from 1907 to 1917. Elizabeth McDougall, notable as the first non-Aboriginal woman to settle in southern Alberta, was a founding member. Alice Jamieson, first female juvenile court judge in the British Commonwealth, served on the board from 1907 to 1932. Other notable women associated with the building include Jessie Chapman who operated the Travellers Aid Society from 1929 to 1961 and Joan Nelson, who spearheaded the campaign to save the building in the late 1970s.

integrity_stmt:
The YWCA building remains in its original location. The building was originally sited on a fairly open space, which has since been encroached on by new construction, including the annex completed to the east in 1955. However, the overall character of the environment with downtown business and high-density residential use has remained consistent.

Although elements of the interior layout have been adjusted to meet continuing usage needs, the overall plan shape and design of the building remain as originally constructed. There have been a number of alterations to both the interior and exterior of the YWCA building since its construction. On the original east façade there was a main-level porch with balconies on the 2nd and 3rd stories; these were removed when the 1954 east annex was constructed. The swimming pool, originally located in the basement of the 1911 building, was closed in 1941 and converted for use as a dormitory in 1943. Residences were remodeled in 1944.  

Further changes were made after the building¿s transfer of ownership to the City of Calgary in 1971. These included the addition of a basement entrance to the right of the main portico, the construction of semi-permanent frame walls to adapt former residences to offices, and structural reinforcements in 1972-1973. At some point prior to 1971, the second floor balcony was removed and replaced with a metal railing; the balusters on the first floor balcony were covered with paneling, and the front two original wood columns on the main portico were replaced with brick piers. The front entrance doors were also replaced around this time.

During the 1980s the brick and sandstone were cleaned and repaired, and further structural repairs were done. Various building upgrades followed in the 1990s, including a security system upgrade and the replacement of the boiler system. The interior woodwork was painted, the office door transoms were covered, and a metal wheelchair ramp was installed in 1999 on the east side of the main entrance. More recently, the roof has been replaced (2010), and the front entrance portico has been entirely reconstructed (2012-2014) to restore a key element of the building¿s original design. 

Overall, there have been continuous modifications to both the interior and exterior of the building; however, since its designation as a provincial historic resource, the interventions, particularly to the exterior of the building, have served to reinforce rather than detract from the overall integrity of the structure.

significance_summ:
This site is significant because...

Palliser Square is tremendously valued as a symbol of the 'New Heart of Downtown Calgary', and was a direct result of urban renewal initiatives to redevelop the downtown core in the 1960s. The property was redeveloped by Marathon Realty, a subsidiary of CPR, established in 1963 to develop CPR land in the Canadian west (Symbolic value - City-wide Significance).

Palliser Square is additionally significant for its revolutionary design as the largest interconnected complex in the Canadian west at the time of its construction. The complex, constructed for $36,000,000, was conceived as a self-sufficient miniature city with internal connecting corridors, stimulating a perception of wholeness (Design value - City-wide significance).

Palliser Square is also valued for its distinctive and cohesive modern style that reflects Classical elements of the original Palliser Hotel architecture through traditional references and the harmonization of materiality, exterior treatments, and scale and massing. The complex was designed by one of Calgary's most talented modern architects, A. Dale & Associates, an architecture, engineering and planning firm (Style value - City-wide significance).

The Palliser Square complex is further valued for its innovative construction techniques involved in building a massive two-block re-development over the existing railway tracks (Construction value - City-wide significance).

Palliser Square also has significant activity value for its role as a principal transportation centre in Calgary. On the historic railway station site, the complex housed the CP Rail passenger station, an Air Canada sales office and travel agency, and the Husky Service Station (Activity value - City-wide significance).

Palliser Square is further significant for its person value in association with Marathon Realty executive, Rod Sykes, head of Marathon Realty and later a successful mayor of Calgary (1969-1977).  Sykes headed up the redevelopment of the CPR land and worked closely with A. Dale & Associates to achieve the modern design for the redevelopment. Sykes' love of archways is expressed in the final design of this complex (Person value - City-wide significance). 

Due to its massive footprint in the downtown core, its prominent siting, and iconic architecture of the Calgary Tower and surrounding buildings, the Palliser Square complex is a landmark development in the City of Calgary (Landmark value - City-wide significance). 

The Husky (Calgary) Tower is evaluated separately as a City Wide Historic Resource.
significance_stmt_dscrn: Palliser Square is a large two-block property containing several interconnected commercial, residential, office, cultural buildings, and a landscaped plaza. The complex was constructed from 1967 to 1971 and is situated on 9th and 10th Avenues between 1st Street SW and 1st Street SE in downtown Calgary. The integrated complex comprises several buildings facing 9th Avenue including: One Palliser Square, a 26-storey office tower; two four-storey commercial complexes (Palliser Square East and West); and the Calgary Tower.  Buildings on 10th Avenue include: the Central Heating and Cooling Plant and Palliser East and West Parkades; the Enterprise Rent-a-Car building (a former gas station); Mount Royal House, a 24-storey residential tower, and the newly constructed Palliser South, an 18-storey tower opened in 2010. The complex of buildings, anchored by the iconic Calgary Tower, is constructed in the modern-style and is harmonized through the use of common materiality such as poured-in-place concrete, pre-cast brick and aggregate panels, Thunderstone cladding as well as the persistent use of arched detailing.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
Palliser Square is valued as a symbol of urban renewal initiatives in the downtown core in the 1960s. The redevelopment of Calgary's CPR depot lands was conceived to attract booming oil companies into new purpose-built towers. The phased plan, with construction beginning in 1965 and complete in 1971, realized demolition of the CPR depot and the building of the Husky Tower; two parking structures; a Heating and Cooling Plant; two commercial complexes, (Palliser Square East and West); a 26-storey office tower (One Palliser Square); a 24-storey apartment complex, (Mount Royal House); and a new CPR train depot. 

The complex is significant for its revolutionary design as the largest interconnected complex in the west at the time of its construction. Constructed for $36,000,000, the complex was conceived as a self-sufficient miniature city with internal connecting corridors. The complex offered internal access to retail, twin theatres, high-end restaurants, a pub, childcare, medical and office space, 202 units of rental apartments, as well as direct access to the Palliser Hotel, and the CP Rail Station. Parking was of high priority for the developers, Marathon Realty, and a parkade was constructed with over 2000 stalls accessed via innovatively designed coiled ramps. 

Palliser Square is also valued for its distinctive and cohesive modern-style architecture. Designed by prominent Calgary-based architecture and engineering firm, A. Dale & Associates, the complex was planned around the Calgary Tower as its central totem. The complex curves back gracefully from the tower and is highly animated through the repetition of flamboyant curves and coils that serve to blunt the contours of the volumes. Materiality is meticulously repeated in the form of board-formed concrete, pre-cast panels of brick and white aggregate, and locally sourced Thunderstone cladding. Formalist embellishments are consistently repeated with Classically inspired fluting at the corners of the buildings, vertical detailing, and handsomely detailed arches that mimic the Classical architecture of the 1914 Palliser Hotel. 

The complex is valued for its innovative construction techniques involved in building a massive two-block re-development over the existing railway tracks. A. Dale employed pioneering building technology through the installation of large neoprene pads on the buildings' foundations to absorb vibration from the nearby rail line. Several of the buildings were constructed without inside columns using a steel I-beam structural system with internal concrete cores and glass curtain walls clad with pre-cast concrete panels. 

Palliser Square has significant activity value for its role as a principal transportation centre. On the historic site of Calgary's train station, the complex housed the CPR passenger station, an Air Canada travel agency, and a Husky Service Station. The new internalized rail station, with no exterior presence, was the first of its kind in Canada and utilized the latest in technology for passengers including conveyor belts for luggage and televisions to monitor incoming trains.

The complex has value for its association with Rod Sykes, head of Marathon Realty, which was established in 1963 by the CPR to develop CPR land in the Canadian west, and later mayor of Calgary (1969-1977). Sykes worked closely with A. Dale on the design of the complex. The ubiquitous archway, repeated throughout the complex, was a design feature favoured by Sykes. Sykes contributed immensely to the first commercial venture of a company that would go on to become one of the largest players in the Canadian development market. 

Due to its massive footprint in the downtown core, its prominent siting, and iconic architecture, the Palliser Square complex is a landmark development in the City of Calgary.

integrity_stmt: The Palliser Square complex is generally in good condition with few major additions or conservation issues.  The white aggregate paneling on many of the buildings is in need of cleaning and several of the precast panels (both brick and aggregate) are cracked or damaged. A new metal mesh fabric system was installed on Heating and Cooling Plant and Palliser East Parkade by Cambridge Architectural in 2008 and this has damaged the visual continuity of the complex. This mesh, however, is removable. Corrugated metal has been added to lower levels of the East Parkade also during this 2008 renovation. These panels are also removable. Corrugated metal has been added for environmental protection to the exterior walls of the parking coils.  The interior of Palliser Square East and West has been completely updated in a 1990s renovation. The interior lobby in One Palliser Square has recently been renovated but the form and massing of the lobby remain intact. The original marble wall tiles and elevators are intact and in good condition.

significance_summ:
The 1913 Northern Electric Co. Warehouse possesses symbolic value for Calgary's early warehouse district located in today's Beltline community. (Symbolic Value, Community Significance)

The building, designed by William John Carmichael (1867-1927), Chief Architect for Northern Electric's parent company Bell Telephone from 1917-27, is valued as an example of the Edwardian Classical style used in industry. (Style Value, Community Significance)

The former distribution warehouse and sales offices, purpose-built and operated by Northern Electric to serve the rapidly growing telecommunications industry for three decades, possesses activity value for its association with that activity. It was later associated with scientific activity for four decades as Canadian Department of Agriculture laboratories. (Activity Value, Community Significance)

The Northern Electric Co. Warehouse is further valued for its association with charitable and social organizations. (Institution Value, Community Significance)
significance_stmt_dscrn: The 1913 Northern Electric Co. Warehouse is a four-storey building of reinforced concrete construction with banks of multi-light windows. Its two lower storeys display stone-look concrete with heavy rusticated piers, deeply recessed windows and horizontal moulded panels between the floors. The upper storeys feature red face-brick cladding articulated by smooth-finished concrete piers that extend to a moulded frieze. The main entryway is a decorative portico. The former warehouse is positioned on a deep corner lot with zero setbacks on the south and west façades, with the main façade fronting 11th Avenue, a busy downtown commercial street and traffic corridor. It is situated just south of the CPR railway right of way, in the part of Beltline originally known as Victoria Park, one of Calgary's earliest inner city communities. The building is located in an area that was historically Calgary's warehouse district.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
The 1913 Northern Electric Co. Warehouse possesses symbolic value for Calgary's early warehouse district located in today's Beltline community. The area where it is located, the northeast part of Beltline, dates to Calgary's early settlement period and was subdivided by the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) in 1885, two years after their transcontinental line reached Calgary. After the CPR also established their north and south railway lines in 1891-92, the city became a major regional distribution centre. A warehouse district developed outwards from the CPR right of way along 10th, 11th and 12th avenues. 
	
By 1913 Northern Electric had acquired a deep parcel fronting 11 AV and backing onto a railway spur line, and engaged Fyshe, McNeill, Martin, Trainer, Engineers & Contractors to erect their four-storey reinforced concrete warehouse. Nova Scotia-born Thomas Maxwell Fyshe was a civil engineer trained at the University of Toronto whose firms were responsible for a number of notable Calgary buildings including Canada Life Assurance and Knox Presbyterian. 

The building, designed by W.J. Carmichael, Chief Architect for Northern Electric's parent company Bell Telephone from 1917-27, is valued as an example of the Edwardian Classical style used in industry. William John Carmichael (1867-1927) was born in Montreal and studied engineering at McGill University. He joined Bell's Montreal headquarters in 1897. As Chief Architect he designed over one hundred telephone exchanges and warehouses, enlivening the industrial-commercial structures with classical detailing. Signatures of Carmichael's designs evident in the building are its boldly-scaled lower concrete walls supporting articulated brick upper walls, deeply recessed windows and an elaborate entrance portico. Other classical features include the heavy rusticated piers which serve as 'bases' for the smooth-finished, upper-storey piers that extend to a moulded frieze. 
 
The former warehouse and offices, purpose-built and operated by Northern Electric to serve the rapidly growing telecommunications industry for three decades, also possesses activity value. When the building opened the firm was relatively new, operating since 1895 when their parent company, Bell Telephone of Canada, made their manufacturing arm an independent corporation. The telephony industry had been growing in Alberta for twenty-five years and Northern Electric provided equipment and knowledge for telephone operators, including Alberta Government Telephones (today's Telus), to build their networks throughout the province. By 1915 the firm was also selling to mutual telephone companies, co-operative rural operators which numbered 600 by 1936. Following the First World War, the company's portfolio expanded to all types of electrical equipment, including products like illumination equipment, theatre sound equipment, and automated alarm systems. Other industry firms like His Master's Voice and Canadian National Carbon had offices in their building. From the late 1950s through 1990 the building was associated with scientific activity when it was adapted for various laboratories run by the Dominion Department of Agriculture. 

The building is also valued for its association with charitable and social organizations. 
In 1942, it had been acquired by the federal government for the war effort and shortly after the war housed the Department of Veterans Affairs which provided Prosthetic Services and ran a Vetcraft shop to employ disabled soldiers. In the 1970s and 1980s it provided space to Canadian Save the Children, a member of Save the Children International, a rights-based organization supporting children worldwide. For the past three decades the building has served the Mustard Seed charity, a faith-based organization first registered in 1984, that provides whole-person services to vulnerable citizens. The building has provided residences, offices, communal space and, for a period, a soup kitchen as well.

The exterior of the Northern Electric Co. Warehouse possesses a high degree of integrity, retaining its form and most of its important architectural features as an Edwardian Classical-style building. The exception is the elaborate, deep cornice lost by 1958, although the loss is mitigated by the moulded frieze which remains. As well, metal lamps and security gates were added to the portico in the 1990s; their design is sympathetic and the change easily reversed. Most of its features as a warehouse building with offices are retained, except the three original very large plate-glass display windows replaced with a double-assembly of smaller windows which is reversible.   

Environment 
The Northern Electric Co. Warehouse retains its situation just south of the CPR railway line and fronting 11th Avenue. Many warehouse buildings remain along 10th, 11th and 12th avenues, and recall the early warehouse district. Its downtown setting has changed, and there are now many tall buildings, especially north of the railway line. A spur line no longer runs along the alley between 10th and 11th avenues, but was still operating until at least the late 1960s.

Materials 
The Northern Electric Co. Warehouse exterior retains most of its original materials, except window sashes, and all of its decorative elements except the cornice. Original 2-over-2 wooden hung window sashes have been replaced by metal sashes (three fixed and one casement) keeping the same configuration of lites. The three large plate-glass display windows, altered by the 1980s, are currently replaced by double assemblies of metal sashes that maintain the same configuration of lites. During works to the exterior 1996-97, including a render coating applied to the two lower storeys. The interior has sustained major renovations since the 1950s, first for laboratories and later for a residences and a commercial kitchen for the Mustard Seed. Almost all the elements of the original office vestibule and stairwell are intact including the tiles under the cover on the stair treads. 

Workmanship 
The Northern Electric Co. Warehouse retains most of its original exterior materials and therefore shows its workmanship, especially the decorative concrete elements and the brick work. The interior also shows craftsmanship in the tile-work and metal work in the original office vestibule and stairwell.

Feeling
The Northern Electric Co. Warehouse retains the feeling of an early 20th Century commercial-industrial building, and recalls the early development of these buildings along the CPR right of way in Connaught and Victoria Park. 

Association
The Northern Electric Co. Warehouse no longer retains its warehouse/sales office activity but retains those associations with its intact exterior, the evidence of the former open arches of the original loading platform and the front stairwell to the original offices. It fully retains its associations with its institutional use, being currently occupied by its long-time owner the Mustard Seed and used to provide services to vulnerable citizens.

significance_summ:
This site is significant because:
-	the building's refined and high-quality facade provides a strong, intact example of Romanesque Revival commercial architecture in Calgary, with some Neoclassical detailing. [Style value: community significance]
-	its contribution to Calgary's historic wholesale/warehouse district, recalls Calgary's historic status as the most important wholesale and distribution centre between Winnipeg and Vancouver. [Activity value: City Wide significance]
-	it contributed to the development of the northern Beltline area as Calgary's main wholesale/warehouse district, and continues to contribute to the warehouse district's historic identity and character. [Symbolic value: community significance]
significance_stmt_dscrn: The Great West Liquor Co. Warehouse, built c. 1911, is a rectangular, two-storey building, of heavy-timber construction clad in brick. Its red-brick facade is enlivened by its rock-faced sandstone detailing and battered foundation, corbelled cornice, and unusual porte-cochere extension. The Romanesque Revival-style warehouse is situated in the northern part of the Beltline community immediately south of Calgary's downtown and contributes to a historic warehouse district adjacent to the Canadian Pacific Railway (C.P.R.) mainline.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
Completed c. 1911, the Great West Liquor Co. Warehouse and its contribution to Calgary's historic wholesale/warehouse district, recalls Calgary's historic status as the most important wholesale and distribution centre between Winnipeg and Vancouver. Due to Calgary's location on both the C.P.R. east-west mainline (established 1883) and the company's important north-south line between Fort Macleod and Edmonton (completed 1892), the city was destined to become a major regional distribution centre. This position was strengthened in 1902 when the railway agreed to offer preferred freight rates on goods shipped from the city. An influx of pioneer settlers and immigrants to the city and region reached a peak from 1909-13 and Calgary thrived as a commercial centre. From Calgary's wholesale district local and national companies supplied the growing city and region with a wide array of merchandise including farm machinery and parts, groceries, dry goods, building supplies and hardware. 

The building was erected c. 1911 for the Great West Liquor Co., which occupied it until 1917. This end date roughly coincides with the enactment of Prohibition legislation in the Alberta in 1916, which caused the demise of local liquor businesses. Starting in 1917, the building was used by a variety of short-term tenants that included a foundry (1917-1920), a wholesale enamelware company (1922-1926), and General Motors Products of Canada Ltd. (1927-1931).

Beginning in 1939, the building housed two long-term co-occupants that were both Calgary branches of national confectionary companies. Walter M. Lowney Company Limited (which occupied the building from 1939 to 1970 and owned it from 1943 to 1970) was a branch of a Montreal-based company. Scott-Bathgate Ltd. (in the building from 1940 to c.1980, its owner from 1970 to 1981) was a branch of a company based in Winnipeg.

The warehouse's refined and high-quality facade provides a strong, intact example of Romanesque Revival-style commercial architecture in Calgary. Romanesque Revival features include the heavily corbelled brick cornice, the battered rock-face (sandstone) foundation, and the rock-faced, sandstone window lintels and sills. An unusual porte-cochere extends from the front corner of the building to provide a secondary entrance which was also a loading dock originally. The building also employs some Neoclassical-style embellishments such as the window keystones and classical profile of the metal cornice of the porte-cochere extension.

The building is of heavy-timber construction and faced with quality red brick.  An illustration from 1911 indicates that it was planned to rise five stories, but with otherwise similar details and features. 

This warehouse contributed to the development of the northern Beltline area as Calgary's main wholesale/warehouse district, and continues to contribute to the warehouse district's historic identity and character. Originally, the principle warehouse district was situated north of the C.P.R. mainline along Eight and Ninth avenues. However, the district along 10th and 11th avenues was established after 1903 when a rail siding off the CPR main line was placed down the alley between 10th and 11th Avenues, from 5th Street SE to  6th Street SW; another siding subsequently and incrementally developed extended from 13th Street SW to 6th St SW. These sidings gave each warehouse along those avenues direct rail access for receiving and shipping cargo via its own rear loading dock. Sixty-four wholesale and warehouse building were situated along both the north and south sides of the C.P.R mainline in 1906, with 160 by 1913. By the later date, however, the majority were located in the northern part of the Beltline. The number of warehouse buildings in the area has been significantly reduced over the years and this warehouse is integral to the remaining group of warehouses and the retention of the area's character which is defined by the warehouses.

On the east elevation, rectangular windows were added to all three stories of after 1981 and a doorway towards the rear has been bricked in. 

On the rear elevation, the center top-storey window had been extended to be a doorway, with sandstone sill removed, by 1981. Rear loading doors have been filled in with blocks. A rear parapet indicated in 1954 maps has either been removed or is not visible from the street.

The interior rear loading area, which once went across the width of the building, had been shortened after 1954 with the addition of a cinderblock wall with metal double-door. A cinderblock storage structure has been attached to its south interior wall. A historic rendering of the building indicates that the porte-cochere was originally used as a loading dock.

All window sashes have been replaced.

The condition of the interior is unknown.

name: Customs House
architect: Chief Architects Branch, Department of Public Works; Leo Dowler (local supervising architect)
development_era: 1906 to 1913 (Pre WWI Boom, Age of Optimism)
significance_stmt_dscrn: The Customs House, completed in 1916, is a four-storey Chicago Commercial-style warehouse-type building, clad with red brick and sandstone.  The Customs House is located in the Beltline neighbourhood immediately south of Calgary's downtown and adjacent to the Canadian Pacific Railway's mainline.
significance_stmt_hrtg_val:
This property is historically significant for its role as the federal government¿s customs house in Calgary from the time of its completion in 1916 until 1979.  During this period it contained the administrative offices and examining quarters for the Port of Calgary.  The Customs House received goods and mail coming into Calgary from foreign places where it was inspected, recorded, and valued for any excise taxes owing prior to re-shipment.  Its location adjacent to the Canadian Pacific Railway's (C.P.R.) mainline and the former site of the C.P.R. station reflects the method of shipment for items historically moving through the Customs House.  The Customs House, which contained the Post Parcels Branch, was strategically situated just two blocks south of the main post office, facilitating the movement of goods between the two buildings.

Largely functioning as a sorting warehouse, the building contained eight administrative offices and a second storey long room - the grand public space of the building.  Indicative of the building's original customs function, the building retains its internal west elevation driveway and loading docks.  Originally, internal driveways and loading docks also comprised the building's north-east corner, but have subsequently been in-filled.

The Customs House is symbolically important, reflecting Calgary's historic status as a major shipping and distribution centre in western Canada.  In 1912, the year it was commissioned, customs receipts in Calgary exceeded those of any other centre west of Toronto, justifying the erection of such a substantial facility.  When completed, the Calgary Customs House was the largest and finest facility of its type between Winnipeg and Vancouver, and equaled facilities in either of those centers.  Further, the Customs House recalls the unprecedented boom that occurred in Calgary between 1909 and 1913, reaching an apex in 1912.  The boom made Calgary one of the fastest growing cities in North America with the Customs House built as a direct result of this activity.  Inauguration of the Customs House replaced customs operations that were housed under no less than five different roofs and continued a tradition of customs services that were first established in Calgary in 1884. 

The Customs House is architecturally significant as Calgary's - if not Alberta's - most handsome example of a warehouse-type structure, and is one of the city's best examples of Chicago Commercial style design.  Similar in design to the Customs Houses in Winnipeg and Vancouver the Customs House exemplifies the customs facilities built by the federal government in large centers prior to the First World War. Classically detailed, it features a rusticated sandstone base, brick-clad upper storeys spanned by pilasters and a substantial, overhanging sheet-metal cornice capping the façades.  Built to be fireproof, the building comprises a steel and concrete frame clad with brick produced on the west side of the City and locally quarried sandstone from the Glenbow area of north-west Calgary.  Canadian made materials and fittings were used in the building's construction to the greatest extent possible, aligning with the period's strong sense of nationalism.  As such, the marble paneling and detailing that still adorns the lobby and staircase of the building was sourced from Quebec quarries.  The Chief Architects Branch of the federal Department of Public Works was responsible for the design.  Leo Dowler, the Dominion Government's Resident Architect in Calgary supervised the construction, with construction charged to the Thomas McDiarmid Co.
